opus-5.5.text:
I think it helps to separate AI research into a few layers, because language models are useful at some layers much more than others right now.

The most immediate layer is engineering. A lot of research time goes into writing training loops, debugging shape mismatches, setting up baselines, sweeping hyperparameters, and making plots. Language models are already genuinely good at this, and in my own work they've compressed what used to take a week into an afternoon. That changes the economics of research: you can afford to try more ideas, including the slightly crazy ones you'd never have bothered implementing before.

The next layer is what I'd call the "scientist's assistant" layer: reading literature, connecting results across papers, proposing experiments, interpreting outcomes. Here models are useful but uneven. They're broad, and they can recall that some trick from physics or numerical analysis might apply to your problem. But they tend to be confident in a way that doesn't track the evidence, and they lean toward conventional ideas, the things that are well represented in their training data. Real breakthroughs often come from noticing something odd that everyone else dismissed, and current models aren't yet great at taking anomalies seriously.

The deepest layer is taste and problem selection: deciding what's worth working on and what counts as understanding. I'm most cautious here. My own interest has always been in interpretability and in science-of-AI questions, where the goal isn't just a number going up but an insight you can explain. If we automate research purely by optimizing benchmarks, we may get a flood of incremental results and lose the understanding. So I'd like to see language models paired with tools that keep things interpretable: symbolic regression, simple toy models, structured representations, so the outputs of automated research are things humans can actually read and verify.

There's also a nice loop here. Interpretability tools make AI systems more legible, and more legible systems are easier for AI to study. So I imagine a future where models help us understand models, and the human role shifts from doing every experiment to being the curator: asking good questions, judging which results are actually meaningful, and keeping a sense of what we're trying to understand in the first place.

So I'm optimistic, but I think the real bottleneck won't be compute or code. It'll be judgment, and that's the part I'd want humans to stay close to for a while.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. This is something I think about a lot, because honestly the day-to-day of AI research is less glamorous than people imagine. A huge fraction of my time goes into things like writing boilerplate training code, debugging a shape mismatch, setting up sweeps, reading forty papers to figure out whether an idea has already been tried. Language models are already very good at that layer, and I use them constantly. That alone probably doubles how many experiments I can run in a week.

But I'd separate two levels. The first is execution: given a clear hypothesis, can the model carry out the experiment, analyze results, and write it up? I think we're close to that being largely automated. In my own work on KANs, for example, a lot of the ablations and visualizations are things I could describe in a paragraph and have a model produce the code for. It's a very capable research assistant.

The second level is taste: deciding which question is worth asking in the first place. That's where I'm more cautious. Good research often comes from noticing that something is weird, or from a strange connection between fields, say, between physics intuition and neural network training. Language models can suggest many ideas, but they tend to suggest the obvious ones, the ones already dense in the literature. Right now they're better at interpolating the space of existing ideas than at finding the empty corners.

That said, I don't think taste is magic. It's partly a product of having run thousands of experiments and seeing what fails. If a model can run thousands of experiments itself and learn from the outcomes, maybe taste emerges too. I find that both exciting and a little unsettling.

So my view is that in the near term, language models turn every researcher into a small lab. Longer term, the interesting question is whether the loop closes, whether the model proposes, tests, and refines its own hypotheses. I think it will, and our job will shift toward asking the questions and judging whether the answers actually mean something.

astra-6.text:
I think language models can help at several levels. They can already help with coding, understanding papers, and designing experiments. That makes the research cycle faster: you have an idea, implement it, look at the results, and decide what to try next.

But the more interesting question is whether they can help us choose better questions. Research is not just finding an answer to a well-defined problem. Often, the difficult part is realizing that the way we framed the problem was wrong, or noticing something unexpected and deciding it deserves attention.

So I would start with a loop where the model proposes hypotheses, runs experiments, and checks its predictions against the results, with a human helping judge which directions matter. The experiments are essential. A convincing explanation is easy to produce; an explanation that survives testing is much more valuable.

Over time, I think more of that loop can be automated. But faster experimentation doesn't automatically mean deeper understanding. That's the distinction I would want to keep in mind.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language models can help at several stages of AI research: reading papers, writing code, designing experiments, and analyzing results. The exciting possibility is connecting those steps into a loop, where a model proposes a hypothesis, runs an experiment, examines what happened, and then revises its hypothesis.

But running that loop is different from doing good research. You need to choose questions that matter and distinguish a meaningful result from an artifact. A model might produce a convincing explanation even when the experiment doesn’t support it, so verification becomes very important.

My expectation is that automation will first make researchers much faster at testing ideas. The deeper question is whether models can develop useful scientific judgment—knowing which assumptions to challenge and which unexpected results deserve attention.
